mcqs.q: Shedding of primary teeth is defined as:
opts: Physiologic loss of deciduous teeth due to progressive root resorption
mcqs.explain: Shedding is the physiologic elimination of deciduous teeth due to progressive root resorption, driven by the pressure of the erupting permanent successor.

mcqs.q: The local factor that initiates shedding is:
opts: Pressure (from the erupting tooth and chewing) that differentiates odontoclasts
mcqs.explain: Local pressure — from the erupting permanent tooth and increased masticatory forces — leads to differentiation of odontoclasts that resorb the root.

mcqs.q: The genetic factor in shedding is evidenced by:
opts: Programmed apoptosis in the periodontal ligament
mcqs.explain: A genetic factor probably initiates root resorption at a specific time, evidenced by programmed cell death (apoptosis) in the periodontal ligament.

mcqs.q: In primary ANTERIOR teeth, root resorption begins on the:
mcqs.explain: Permanent anteriors lie apico-lingual to their predecessors, so resorption of the primary anterior root begins on the apico-lingual surface and proceeds apically.

mcqs.q: In primary MOLARS, root resorption first begins on the:
mcqs.explain: Premolars develop between the divergent roots of the primary molars, so resorption begins on the inner (interradicular) surfaces.

mcqs.q: The cells that resorb the hard dental tissues during shedding are:
mcqs.explain: Odontoclasts remove the hard dental tissues (dentin, cementum and even enamel) during root resorption.

mcqs.q: Odontoclasts share their origin with osteoclasts, namely:
mcqs.explain: Odontoclasts have the same origin as osteoclasts — monocytes or undifferentiated mesenchymal cells — and are structurally identical to them.

mcqs.q: A structural feature of the odontoclast facing the surface being resorbed is the:
mcqs.explain: Odontoclasts are large multinucleated cells with foamy cytoplasm and a ruffled (brush) border facing the surface being resorbed.

mcqs.q: Odontoclasts occupy shallow scalloped depressions of the root surface called:
mcqs.explain: Odontoclasts line up in hollowed-out, scalloped depressions of the root known as Howship's lacunae (the same as in bone resorption).

mcqs.q: The correct sequence of resorption of dental hard tissue is:
opts: Demineralization by acids, then organic matrix degradation by proteolytic enzymes
mcqs.explain: Odontoclasts first remove minerals (acids), then degrade the organic matrix (proteolytic enzymes).

mcqs.q: During shedding, the periodontal ligament fibroblasts:
opts: Undergo apoptosis with abrupt loss of PDL (without inflammation)
mcqs.explain: PDL fibroblasts show impaired function with abrupt loss of the ligament and programmed cell death (apoptosis), without signs of inflammation.

mcqs.q: The role of the pulp during shedding is:
opts: Passive — it appears histologically normal (only neural elements lost)
Formation of new dentin to stop shedding
mcqs.explain: The pulp does not contribute to shedding and plays a passive role; it appears histologically normal except for loss of neural elements.

mcqs.q: A deciduous tooth whose eruption has stopped, sitting below the level of adjacent teeth, is:
opts: A submerged tooth (usually due to ankylosis)
mcqs.explain: A submerged tooth has stopped active eruption and lies lower than its neighbours, usually because of ankylosis.

mcqs.q: Ankylosis of a tooth is:
opts: A bony union between the alveolar bone and the root
mcqs.explain: Ankylosis is a bony union between the alveolar bone and the tooth root (e.g. after mild PDL trauma); submerged ankylosed teeth should be removed.

mcqs.q: Retained deciduous teeth are MOST common as the:
opts: Upper canine ('B') and lower second molar ('E')
mcqs.explain: Retained deciduous teeth (persisting beyond the normal shedding age) are most common in the upper B (canine) and lower E (second molar).

mcqs.q: A common cause of a retained deciduous tooth is:
mcqs.explain: Causes include congenitally missing teeth (hypodontia — often lateral incisors and second premolars), impaction of the permanent tooth, and ankylosis of the successor.

mcqs.q: Remnants of deciduous teeth (retained root tips) occur because:
opts: Root parts off the eruption path escape resorption
mcqs.explain: Parts of deciduous roots not in the path of the erupting permanent tooth may escape resorption and remain deep in the bone (e.g. the widely divergent roots of the lower E).

mcqs.q: The possible fate of a retained deciduous root tip includes all EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: A retained root tip may be surrounded by cellular cementum, ankylose to bone, resorb and disappear, or exfoliate — it cannot become a permanent tooth.

mcqs.q: The radiographic/clinical appearance of a resorbing primary molar shows:
opts: Shortened roots with resorption lacunae as the successor erupts beneath
mcqs.explain: A resorbing primary molar shows progressively shortened roots with resorption lacunae as the underlying premolar erupts toward it.

mcqs.q: Odontoclasts are stimulated to begin root resorption by:
opts: Pressure from the erupting permanent teeth
mcqs.explain: Odontoclasts are stimulated by the pressure exerted by the erupting permanent teeth, then line up along the root surface in Howship's lacunae.

saqs.q: Define shedding and state what initiates it.
saqs.a: Physiologic loss of deciduous teeth by progressive root resorption, driven by pressure of the erupting successor (local factor) and a genetic factor (PDL apoptosis).

saqs.q: Describe the pattern of resorption for anterior teeth and molars.
saqs.a: Anteriors: begins on the apico-lingual root surface. Molars: begins on the inner (interradicular) surfaces (premolars lie between the divergent roots).
Origin: monocytes / UMC (like osteoclasts). Structure: large, multinucleated, foamy cytoplasm, ruffled border. Location: root surface in Howship's lacunae.

saqs.q: Outline the two steps of hard-tissue resorption.
saqs.a: 1. Demineralization by acids, then 2. organic matrix degradation by proteolytic enzymes (both by odontoclasts).

saqs.q: What happens to the PDL and pulp during shedding?
saqs.a: PDL: fibroblasts undergo apoptosis (no inflammation) with abrupt loss of the ligament. Pulp: stays normal and is passive (only loses neural elements).

saqs.q: What are submerged teeth and their cause?
saqs.a: Teeth whose eruption has stopped, lying below adjacent teeth, due to ankylosis (bony union of root and bone) — they should be removed.
Submerged (ankylosed) teeth, retained deciduous teeth, and remnants/retained root tips.
